summary:
Gümüşhane Province stands under the national framework of Turkey, which governs visitors in Gümüşhane. The sources record no provincial legal divergence from that frame, so a trans visitor to the province should expect the national pattern of law, document handling and policing rather than any local variant.

Homosexuality has not been treated as a criminal offence in Turkey since the Ottoman Empire's 1858 penal code. Transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988, and gender-reassignment surgery has been legal since 1988 subject to court-approved procedures.

No comprehensive law in Turkey prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Same-sex relationships receive no legal recognition: the law defines marriage as a union between a man and a woman, which makes same-sex marriage legally impossible though not criminalised, and the gender recorded on a trans person's civil-registry record determines their marriage eligibility.

A leaked omnibus draft known as the 11th Judicial Package, reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025, would amend the penal and civil codes to criminalise LGBT conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality, carrying up to 3 years' imprisonment, and to criminalise same-sex ceremonies with up to 4 years.

The same draft would raise the age for gender-affirming healthcare to 25 and impose mandatory infertility and multiple-evaluation conditions, while punishing providers with fines and up to 7 years' imprisonment. Fifteen LGBT groups and the national medical association have objected to the package.

Authorities have banned Pride events in Istanbul and other cities in most years since 2015, with police using tear gas and water cannons. Amnesty International reported restrictions and excessive force against Pride protesters in 2015 and in 2024.
tangentialFactors:
The decriminalisation of homosexuality dates to the Ottoman Empire's 1858 penal code, and legal gender change and gender-reassignment surgery have been available since 1988; both provisions predate the current political climate and do not indicate a permissive environment in practice.

Pride bans have applied in most years since 2015 across Istanbul and several other Turkish cities, with tear gas and water cannon used against participants. Amnesty International documented restrictions and excessive force in 2015 and again in 2024, indicating that the pattern of prohibition and force spans a decade rather than a single episode.

The sources record no provincial legal divergence for Gümüşhane, so the province is a data point confirming the national pattern rather than a separate regime.

The gender recorded on a trans person's civil-registry record determines their marriage eligibility, because marriage is legally defined as a union between a man and a woman. Same-sex marriage is legally impossible though not criminalised.

If enacted as drafted, the 11th Judicial Package would raise the age for gender-affirming healthcare to 25 and add mandatory infertility and multiple-evaluation conditions, restricting transition care for residents as well as visitors, and would expose healthcare providers to fines and up to 7 years' imprisonment.

outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the 11th Judicial Package has been enacted, amended or withdrawn since it was reported as a leaked draft on 29 October 2025 is unresolved in the sources supplied; the inventory describes it as a draft with objections pending.

No Gümüşhane-specific material was supplied on local policing, checkpoint practice, hospitals providing transition care, or documented incidents affecting trans people in the province. The province-level source records no further finding, so the province profile rests entirely on the national framework.

Whether the 1988 provisions on legal gender change and surgery have been modified by post-2018 legal changes is not addressed in this inventory.
